power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFRrelated conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes.
These 30 mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes.
This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies.
We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and nonsyndromic non-FGFR-related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework.
We 35 analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non-syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls.
Millimetric 3D T1-weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist).
After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power-law model, effect of brain 40 size regardless of age) were derived in controls.
Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles).
Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size.
Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones.
Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size.
Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size.

Our findings reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related 50 craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal-frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and nonsyndromic patients.

Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work 55 highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

Craniosynostoses are congenital craniofacial malformations resulting from the premature 60 fusion of one or more cranial and/or facial sutures, leading to abnormal skull shape and potentially impaired brain development and growth (Yasaroglu & Demir, 2023).

text.text: Some forms of craniosynostoses are associated with mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) gene group (Webster & Donoghue, 1997), such as Crouzon syndrome, Apert syndrome, and Muenke syndrome.

text.text: Their prevalence varies, with Crouzon syndrome 65 occurring in 1/50,000 to 1/60,000 live births (Helman et al., 2014), Apert syndrome in 1/65,000 (Breik et al., 2016), and Muenke syndrome being more common at 1/10,000 births (Sabatino et al., 2004).

text.text: Besides these rare syndromic forms, non-syndromic craniosynostoses are much more common and occur in 5.2 of every 10,000 live births.

In these conditions, the skull malformation occurs in isolation, with no identified mutation or 70 evident extra-cranial phenotypic expression in most cases, particularly without known specific cerebral phenotype (Alperovich et al., 2025).

text.text: Syndromic craniosynostoses are characterized by extensive phenotypic features including cranial, facial, cerebral and extracephalic features.
Each syndrome presents with distinctive cranial abnormalities.

Crouzon syndrome is characterized by midface 75 hypoplasia (Levesque et al., 2019) and is associated with variability in suture closure, with different sutures affected to different degrees depending on the patient (Azoury et al., 2017) leading to variable levels of skull growth anomalies (Delassus, 2025).

text.text: Apert syndrome also features midface hypoplasia and is generally associated with bicoronal craniosynostosis (Giancotti et al., 2014).

text.text: Muenke syndrome generally has a less severe facial involvement and 80 is associated with bicoronal craniosynostosis in most cases (Mathijssen, 2015).

text.text: The cerebral phenotype of syndromic craniosynostoses is less clearly defined that the skeletal phenotype and varies in severity regarding brain structure and cognitive functions.

Surgical interventions may influence outcomes (Mathijssen, 2015), but a cognitive and behavioral phenotype is frequently observed despite optimal management that may lead to 85 severe neurodevelopmental impairment (Mathijssen, 2015).

text.text: The functional phenotype in Crouzon syndrome is varied and imprecisely documented, visual impairment affecting up to 40% of patients (Bowling & Burstein, 2006), and hearing loss in 74% (Agochukwu et al., 2014).

text.text: In addition, recurrent neurological abnormalities are associated with these conditions.

In Crouzon syndrome, intracranial hypertension occurs in 40-63% of cases (Levesque et al., 2019), (Spruijt et al., 2016), as well as ventriculomegaly (38-70%) (Doerga et al., 2022), hydrocephalus (29%) (Coll et al., 2015), and Chiari I malformations (70%) (Cinalli et al., 2005).

text.text: Muenke syndrome has been related to an increase in the volume of the posterior fossa and 100 cerebellum (Rijken et al., 2015).

text.text: Nevertheless, although these syndromes differ clinically, they share a close genetic relationship through activating mutations affecting FGFR genes (FGFR2 and FGFR3).
These mutations notably lead to bone abnormalities and premature fusion of cranial sutures (Azoury et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These mutations notably lead to bone abnormalities and premature fusion of cranial sutures <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Azoury et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Both FGFR2 and FGFR3 alternatively splice their mRNA, producing 105 isoforms that bind different fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) (Galzie et al., 1997), this ligandbinding specificity being crucial for embryonic development and organogenesis.

text.text: Most FGFR2 mutations occur in exons IIIa and IIIc, essential regions for receptor function (Chim et al., 2011), the FGFR2c isoform (alternative exon IIIc) being particularly expressed in the mesenchymal tissues forming the flat bones of the developing skull (Chim et al., 2011).

text.text: A 110 large diversity of pathogenic FGFR2 variants is responsible for Crouzon syndrome while in Apert syndrome, p.S252W and p.P253R elective mutations alter the ligand affinity of FGFR2c (Chim et al., 2011), enabling abnormal binding to specific FGFs.

text.text: In addition to osteogenesis, FGFs are also involved in brain development, neuronal maturation, neuroprotection and neurometabolic regulation.
For example, FGF1 and FGF2 contribute to neuronal growth and 115 plasticity, with FGF2 also stimulating osteogenesis (Reuss et al., 2003).

text.text: Therefore, activating FGFR mutations is expected to affect both skull morphogenesis and brain development, underlying the intricate phenotypes observed in these syndromes.
Despite these insights, the cerebral phenotype associated with FGFR-related craniosynostoses remains poorly understood, and epidemiological and clinical data are 120 rare.
Neuroimaging research based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has just begun to explore brain structure with more details.

A recent study reported that patients with FGFR mutations had increased intracranial volume compared to controls, while displaying relatively reduced cortical surface area, particularly in the parietal and occipital lobes (Wilson et al., 2022).

text.text: The existing literature, however, reveals contradictory results.

Studies 125 of intracranial and cerebral volumes in craniosynostosis have reported heterogeneous results, ranging from increased volumes in some syndromes (Dubois et al., 2008) to normal volumes in others (Junn et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Studies 125 of intracranial and cerebral volumes in craniosynostosis have reported heterogeneous results, ranging from increased volumes in some syndromes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dubois et al., 2008)</ref> to normal volumes in others <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Junn et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These divergences may be attributed to variations in the types of syndromes, sample sizes and imaging methodologies.
Overall, these observations highlight important lacunae in our understanding of the brain patterns 130 associated with FGFR mutations.
Indeed, understanding the mechanisms of brain disruption in FGFR-related craniosynostosis syndromes presents several challenges.
Firstly, it is essential to improve our knowledge and description of observable brain abnormalities associated with the different syndromes.

Secondly, it is crucial to distinguish the congenital cerebral alterations from secondary complications linked to the progression 135 of the disease or the side-effects of therapeutic wandering and surgical treatments.
Finally, identifying correlations between genotype and brain phenotype remains an essential objective for advancing diagnosis and personalized management.

Today, tertiary expert centers are able to gather relatively large clinical series of genotyped and perisurgically-imaged patients, allowing the study of the neuroanatomical phenotype of 140 these syndromes in greater depth, while carefully controlling for confounding factors.

Object-based neuroimaging strategies relying on a limited set of robust regions of interest and anatomic parameters (volumes, surfaces), combined with normative analysis methods (Marquand, 2016), are expected to be sensitive enough to detect individual brain abnormalities associated with FGFR2 or 3 pathogenic variants, such as global or focal 145 abnormalities in brain growth (size-for-age), or even abnormalities in brain scaling (size distribution among regions) independent of a global sizing (Fraize et al. 2023; Kerdreux et al., 2025).

text.text: Using a clinical MRI dataset of patients with craniosynostosis, including patients with Crouzon, Apert and Muenke syndromes but also patients with non-syndromic 150 presentations, imaged before or close to first surgical step, and a large group of typically developing controls, we segmented, quality-checked and harmonized 8 cerebral volumes of interest at the scale of large cerebral regions.
Firstly, we established typical normograms on controls, based on growth (cross-sectional effect of age) and static scaling models (size effect independent from age).
Secondly, we tested whether the patient groups showed 155 global or regional deviations from the volumes expected for their age.

In a third step, we regressed out the age parameter, under the assumption of z-score stability during growth, and tested whether the patient groups showed regional deviations from the expected volume for brain size.

AssemblyNet provided a 200 BrainCOLOR-based detailed volumetric parcellation of the cortex which was merged into 6 cortical regions: frontal, central, temporal, parietal, occipital, and insula.

Two steps of regularization of these parcels were performed to remove improper cross boundary labelling (for instance across sulcal boundaries): a volume-based one (one sequence of erosion, sulcal skeleton exclusion, largest component selection, dilation) and a surface-based one 205 after projection of the parcels on the inner cortical surface (one sequence of erosiondilation).
Deep gray matter and brainstem were merged into a 'braincore' (regularized by morphological closure).

The six cortical surface parcels were ultimately back-projected into the brain volume and expanded within the hemispheres to the braincore boundaries (multilabel front propagation) to define 6 volumetric hemispheric ROIs.

Our study proposed a normative approach based on a rare set of clinical MRI to analyze cerebral volumetric regional profiles in syndromic craniosynostosis linked to FGFR2 and FGFR3 mutations.

Our results highlighted syndrome specific cerebral alterations, particularly a contrasting pattern of growth and sizing (static-scaling) anomalies common to Apert and Muenke syndromes, albeit with a smaller effect size for the latter.

Conversely, both patients with Crouzon syndrome and non-syndromic patients showed brain volume distributions close to typical individuals, with the mild singularities identified being similar in both conditions.

In addition to a contribution to a better understanding of craniosynostosis linked to FGFR variants, our results also illustrate the potential of clinical data inscribed into a methodological framework exploiting the current reference datasets and harmonization tools.
The results indicated that Apert syndrome was associated with significant global and regional volumetric abnormalities.

Apart from an enlargement of the lateral ventricles, the total brain parenchyma was overgrown so as the temporal lobes, consistent with some rare reports from the literature (increased intracranial volume (Wilson et al., 2022), temporal lobe abnormalities (Raybaud & Di Rocco, 2007)).

text.text: Notably, this overgrowth also concerned other brain regions, such as particularly the cerebellum, but spared the frontal lobes.

These differences were ultimately reflected in an atypical distribution of brain volume for brain size, with oversized temporal and cerebellar regions and relatively undersized frontal regions (for a brain of this size).

As such, it may be interesting to look at this uneven distribution from another point of view, taking the frontal lobe -of expected size for age -as a reference, which highlights a gradient of oversizing for the rest of the cerebral regions in Apert syndrome, of which the temporal and, to a lesser extent, the cerebellar regions constitute the extrema (see this representation in Supplementary Material, Sup.
Figure S5).

text.text: Indeed, the very small number of patients with Apert syndrome, (n=4) constituting more a small case series than a representative group of the Apert syndrome population, tends to weaken these results.
Their significance was supported by large effect sizes, but a selection bias is difficult to rule out.
However, it should be remembered that the only active selection made was on the quality of the MRI scans and their compatibility with the proposed computational treatments.
With this in mind, the intra-group consistency of the anomalies and their concordance with the literature reinforced their reliability.

More unexpectedly, as suggested by no preliminary data, our analyses revealed a rather similar, albeit less intense, pattern of volumetric anomalies in Muenke syndrome, with temporal « overgrowth » and oversizing, associated with frontal undersizing for brain size.

Here again, the small size of the group (n=6) makes the result prone to an even « random » selection bias , but the consistency over the 6 subjects seems an element of conviction. Interestingly, in a context where we could not detect any global « overgrowth » of the brain, the static-scaling analysis revealed an atypical pattern of volume distribution similar to the one observed in Apert syndrome.

text.text: By contrast, patients with Crouzon syndrome showed only ventricular abnormalities, with almost no significant cortical or subcortical volumetric alterations for age and a mild uneven distribution of brain volumes for brain size, a configuration eventually very similar to the one observed in non-syndromic craniosynostoses.

The size of these two groups might suggest a lower risk of insufficient sampling of the population, Yet, given the heterogeneity at least of Crouzon syndrome compared with Apert and Muenke syndromes both genetically (large diversity of FGFR2 variants in Crouzon syndrome, virtually unknown determinism in non-445 syndromic craniosynostosis) and phenotypically (among other things, diversity of sutural anomalies) -we could have under-sampled subgroups and masked their specific effects.
Qualitative observation of the data or distribution tests did not support this hypothesis, which would nevertheless require larger numbers to be effectively tested.

Furthermore, complementary analysis of the Crouzon syndrome and non-syndromic groups restricted to patients with bicoronal anomalies did not support an effect of sutural phenotype on cerebral parameters in our patients.

Yet this pattern of regional brain growth and scaling rather similar to typically developing controls in patients with Crouzon syndrome might look surprising given the high frequency of neurological symptoms reported in this condition, such as raised intracranial pressure (Spruijt et al., 2016), Chiari (Cinalli et al., 2005) or neurodevelopment impairments (Wenger et al., 2020 , Wilson, 2020).

text.text: The ventricle enlargement was almost expected and of course limited in amplitude by the fact that we excluded the patient with more than mild ventriculomegaly.

The mild frontal oversizing for brain size common with non-syndromic forms -probably at the expense of the temporaloccipital regions according to the pattern trending in the two average z-score maps -might be more informative and an avenue for further studies, though it could only be the residual of an abusive averaging between more contrasted subgroup effects.

From a clinical perspective, it makes sense that we found the main growth and sizing regional anomalies in the brain of the patients with the two syndromes more associated with neurodevelopmental disorders (50% of intellectual development disorder in Apert syndrome, 40% in Muenke syndrome with 20% epilepsy (Kruszka et al., 2016).

text.text: Here we excluded Crouzon syndrome patients with severe initial presentations such as cloverleaf skulls, where brain malformations may be present.

For instance, a neuropathological investigation of fetuses with FGFR2-related syndromic craniosynostoses diagnosed as Pfeiffer syndrome (now considered as a variant of Crouzon syndrome) have reported temporal lobe malformations that reminded the malformations observed in FGFR3-related thanatophoric dysplasia, a lethal form of chondrodysplasia (Hevner et al., 2005 , Khonsari et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For instance, a neuropathological investigation of fetuses with FGFR2-related syndromic craniosynostoses diagnosed as Pfeiffer syndrome (now considered as a variant of Crouzon syndrome) have reported temporal lobe malformations that reminded the malformations observed in 485 FGFR3-related thanatophoric dysplasia, a lethal form of chondrodysplasia <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hevner et al., 2005</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">, Khonsari et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of brain phenotype we report may thus be related to a selection bias.

Nevertheless, extremely severe presentations such as cloverleaf skulls are not the most common clinical situation in this syndrome and our results, both for Crouzon syndrome and non-syndromic craniosynostoses, are in line with the fact that these two conditions have generally milder cognitive alterations than Apert and Muenke syndrome patients.

Genetically speaking, the converging pattern observed in Apert and Muenke syndromes, if confirmed on a larger number of subjects, is both unexpected and questioning from a mechanistic point of view, given that these syndromes are linked to very specific variants but in two different genes of the FGFR family.

Although it is not possible to consider this type of correlation in our dataset, it is now possible to test whether greater deviations from typical brain growth or regional dimensioning is associated with greater severity of the neurodevelopmental disorders associated with these two syndromes.
Conversely, the apparent consistency of the absence of any major neuroanatomical abnormality in the Crouzon syndrome spectrum shall not hinder from questioning the relevance of this finding.

Indeed, the high heterogeneity of genetic variants in Crouzon syndrome compared with syndromes such as Apert syndrome (2 causal variants) or Muenke syndrome (only one) could account for the absence of a homogeneous trend towards regionalized brain volumetric dysgenesis.

It is also possible that all the FGFR2 variants involved in Crouzon syndrome share a relative lack of effect on brain growth (which would not exclude them having common or specific effects on other aspects of brain development or maturation), compared to the two Apert syndrome variants for instance.
To better understand this point, the spectrum of Crouzon syndrome shall probably described regarding the cognitive phenotype and its correlations with neuroanatomy and genotype.
As mentioned above, the most severe variants of Crouzon syndrome in our cohort have been excluded from this study.
Crouzon syndrome patients with cloverleaf skull and/or severe and early hydrocephalus do not have a specific genetic background reported to date.

Despite this current limitation in the characterization of the cohort, a stratification of Crouzon syndrome patients according to cognitive status could still contribute to tackle an important question raised by our study.

In fact, the brain malformations we report in Apert and Muenke syndromes could be: (1) common to all patients with FGFR mutations and severe brain involvement, including the excluded forms of severe Crouzon syndrome patients, or (2) relate to specific, still undescribed, mechanisms common to Muenke and Apert syndromes but not present in Crouzon syndrome.
According to the current, very limited, available date in the literature, the first hypothesis seems the most relevant.

In fact, as mentioned above, severe prenatal forms of FGFR2-related Crouzon syndrome (labeled as Pfeiffer syndrome) have been associated with major brain malformations resembling malformation in other conditions due to activating FGFR mutations such as FGFR3-related thanathophoric dysplasia.

Furthermore, the very uncommon subtype of Crouzon syndrome due to FGFR3 mutations (Crouzon with acanthosis nigricans) seems to be associated with specific clinical severity and brain anomalies (Cornille et al., 2022 , de Planque et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the very uncommon subtype of Crouzon syndrome 525 due to FGFR3 mutations (Crouzon with acanthosis nigricans) seems to be associated with specific clinical severity and brain anomalies <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cornille et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">, de Planque et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These phenotypic overlaps in conditions due to different mutations may be related to the expression overlap of FGFR genes in the craniofacial region, both in humans and in mouse models.

In brief, as there is no current argument to relate the mechanisms underlying Apert and Muenke syndromes, the proximity of their brain phenotype may correspond to the characterization of the severe side of a common spectrum of brain anomalies due to all activating FGFR mutations (Delezoide et al., 1998 , Paek et al., 2009).

text.text: Furthermore, even though the genetics causes of the vast majority of non-syndromic craniosynostosis cases are still to be uncovered, several mutations have been associated with specific risks of cognitive impairment and potential brain anomalies (Timberlake et al., 2022).

text.text: The non-syndromic group also shall benefit from more precise neuroanatomical characterization in relation with functional severity before being considered as a control group where the sole source of anomalies is the skull deformation.

Finally, our results also suggest that the genotype has a predominant influence on cerebral organization in craniosynostoses compared with the sutural phenotype, which could have played a direct role (by simple deformation or even developmental stress), or else be an indirect marker of cerebral dysgenesis.

Indeed, even when restricting the analysis to patients with bicoronal synostosis, no convergence in volumetric pattern emerged between the Crouzon syndrome group (and the non-syndromic patients) and the Apert syndrome or Muenke syndrome groups.
Also, the post-hoc analysis performed on the Crouzon syndrome patients did not show any major differences between the Crouzon syndrome subgroups according to the suture affected.
Neuroimaging research into rare conditions such as syndromic craniosynostosis is complicated by the lack of access to sufficient quality data in sufficient quantity.

Our approach has been to combine a number of methodological tools implemented in recent years for neuroanatomical analysis in computational imaging, in order to make the most of the rare retrospective data set at our disposal.

The main strategy had been to generate normograms reflecting the effect of age (cross-sectional) and size (static-scaling) in the context of typical development, which would be accurate enough and compatible with our patient data.

To achieve this, we combined data harmonization tools, whose effectiveness in computational neuroanatomy has been widely documented, with explicit modeling of normative curves by rather simple biomathematical functions (few parameters to fit), which are relatively data-saving.
In terms of harmonizing data by correcting for batch effects, the main weakness of our approach lay in the heterogeneous nature of the patient acquisition site (NEM site).

Indeed, even though the same panel of 3DT1 sequences was used for patients and controls from the NEM site, it was not possible to divide this site into as many sequences for the sake of parametrization.

This is why we sought to verify whether this choice did not bias the analysis of mean divergence from the normative model obtained on all controls by a post-hoc test based on a partition of controls from the NEM site: none of the four partitions of eight controls considered as a group of interest (pseudo-patient) showed significant deviation from the norm for any of the anatomical metrics studied, validating the hypothesis that, within the precision limits of the study, our simplification of the batch effect model remained acceptable.

More generally, it would have been preferable to have more homogeneous data in terms of 3DT1 sequence parameterization, over and above the multisite character, even though the large neuroanatomical objects we studied are probably little sensitive to sequence effects due to the dilution of the small differences induced in the total volume of the object (unlike cortical objects, for example).

Despite our reassuring post-hoc verifications, taking into account the sequence effect through the site effect is probably not optimal, but it is important to bear in mind the size of the main effects finally observed, particularly in the Apert and Muenke syndromes group, which it is hardly debatable and exceeds the magnitude of the noise or even the residual biases linked to the production of the normograms.
Regarding the modelling of age and size effects, the power law choice for scaling analysis rather consensual and its use was highly documented, including from our previous work.
Modeling age effect forms a 130 subject large control group over a 16 years window with a rather simple (parsimonious parametrization) function is a less well-documented task.

Interestingly, classical growth curves such as von Bertalanffy didn't show convincing fits, with nearly asymptotic values reached as early as 4 to 5 years of age, which was not consistent with the literature (Peterson et al., 2018).

text.text: We chose to rely on a more general model published by Turner and providing sufficient degree of freedom to fit a more convincing "growth" dynamic from our data set at the extent of only 3 parameters to fit.

Eventually, within the limits of the available power, we found the residual from our models to show no heteroscedasticity, allowing for rather easy estimate of z-score and proper uses of the proposed statistics.

Concerns about the sample size, particularly for Apert and Muenke syndromes, and about the setting-up of normative charts have been already mentionned but two important built-in limitations have still to be taken into.

First, we wanted to study the brains of patients with the least impact on development from mechanical complications such as hydrocephalus, or from the often-cumbersome therapeutic sequences, which also degrades the quality of brain images.
For the sake of recruitment, we did include data from MRI performed before surgery, but also just in the aftermath of the first surgical step (may the only).

This pragmatic and developmentally relevant choice nevertheless reduces the representativeness of the data, associated with the de facto exclusion of the large number of children who required early surgery, at an age when only T2 weighted images were available, which is often not usable (clinical 2D imaging) and in any case requires very different analysis strategies.
Besides, potential effect of the first step of surgical procedures cannot be totally ruled out, even if a comparison between pre-and post-operative Crouzon syndrome (see supplementary material Sup.
